paper.citation: Barber-Westin S, Noyes FR. Blood Flow-Restricted Training for Lower Extremity Muscle Weakness due to Knee Pathology: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2018.
paper.abstract: Systematic review of controlled trials (9 studies: 8 level 1, 1 level 2; 165 BFRT and 170 control participants) of blood flow-restricted training for knee-related lower extremity weakness or atrophy, or for atrophy after knee surgery. The literature search covered PubMed and Cochrane databases from 1974 to 2017.
paper.tldr: Limited trials suggest blood flow-restricted training is safe and may improve quadriceps strength in knee-related weakness, but cuff pressure, dose and duration are not settled and the evidence is small.
paper.methods: PRISMA-guided systematic review of PubMed and Cochrane databases for controlled trials of BFRT for chronic knee-related atrophy or for atrophy after knee surgery. The search identified 534 articles, 525 were excluded, and 9 studies were included; quality was rated with PEDro for randomised studies and MINORS for non-randomised studies.
paper.findings: Six of seven studies measuring quadriceps strength reported significant improvements after BFRT, and BFRT produced larger gains than controls in three investigations. Quadriceps cross-sectional area showed few benefits, hamstrings were measured in only two studies, and no complications were reported.
paper.limitations: Only 9 heterogeneous studies were included, with varied cuff pressures, exercise protocols and outcomes. Only 4 studies performed power analyses, few reported effect sizes, and the authors note some significant results may have limited clinical relevance.
paper.practicalImplications: BFRT may be considered as an adjunct to quadriceps strengthening in selected knee patients, using low loads (about 30% 1RM) with short-duration occlusion, which the review found to be safe after knee surgery or in arthritic knees. Protocols are not standardised, so a single cuff pressure or dose should not be assumed from these studies.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not test performance outcomes in healthy or trained athletes, since trained healthy participants and athletes were excluded. It can inform strength rebuilding in athletes with knee pathology only as low-certainty evidence.
paper.rtp: The review gives limited support for BFRT as an adjunct to quadriceps strengthening after ACL reconstruction or knee arthroscopy. It does not assess return-to-sport criteria or sport function and cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to play.
